chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Selling an inherited property blends emotions and legal steps. Between settling the estate, decisions among several heirs and the tax aspects, it's best to move forward methodically and with good support.

This guide maps out the main stages: the liquidator's role, the checks before selling, the tax issues to know, and managing decisions among heirs.

Informational content, not legal or tax advice: surround yourself with a notary and, if needed, an accountant. Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

Selling an inherited property blends law, taxation, logistics and emotions. This guide clarifies who can sell and when, how to prepare and price the property, the tax issues, decisions among several heirs, and the delicate step of emptying the house.

Goal: carry out the sale calmly, by the rules, without conflict or emotion costing you value.

chapters.title: The liquidator's role and the prerequisites
chapters.objective: Knowing who can sell and when.
chapters.html:
Knowing who can sell and when.

In an estate, it's generally the liquidator (formerly “executor”) who administers the assets and carries out the sale, according to the will and the law. Certain steps must precede the sale (settling the estate, publishing documents in the register).

  • Confirm who the liquidator is and their powers.
  • Check the title of ownership and the registration in the Land Register.
  • Understand what the will provides for the property.

In an estate, it's generally the liquidator who has the power to sell, once certain steps are completed (acceptance of the office, inventory, sometimes authorizations). Check who is authorized and what prerequisites are required BEFORE going to market, to avoid a challengeable sale.

Emilie's tip

Before even thinking about price, have the notary confirm who has the power to sell and what steps must be completed. Selling too early or without the right powers creates costly blockages.

chapters.title: Preparing the property and setting the price
chapters.objective: Selling a property that's often old or unoccupied.
chapters.html:
Selling a property that's often old or unoccupied.

An inherited property is sometimes aging, furnished or unoccupied for a while. Prepare it like any sale: empty it, clean, fix the essentials, then set a price backed by a comparative analysis.

  • Have the current market value assessed (CMA).
  • Decide what to empty, repair or sell as is.
  • Consider an inspection to know the real condition and avoid disputes.

An inherited property is often old, furnished or unoccupied: a cleaning, a declutter and a few targeted repairs can markedly improve the price. Set the price on a comparative analysis, not on sentimental value or the municipal assessment.

Emilie's tip

Don't sell an inherited property cheap out of haste, but don't over-invest in renovations either. Light preparation and a fair price often give the best net result for the heirs.

chapters.title: The tax issues to know
chapters.objective: Anticipating the tax tied to the estate and the sale.
chapters.html:
Anticipating the tax tied to the estate and the sale.

The taxation of an inherited property can be complex: depending on the case, a capital gain may be calculated from the value at death, the principal residence may qualify for an exemption, etc. The rules depend on the specific situation.

Assume nothing: an accountant or tax specialist, together with the notary, will tell you what applies and how to minimize the tax legally.

The taxation of an estate can be complex: capital gain, value at death, deadlines. A mistake can be costly. Consult a notary and an accountant to understand the implications before selling — it's an investment that avoids nasty tax surprises.

Emilie's tip

Talk to an accountant BEFORE selling, not after. An estate's tax decisions have to be planned: once the sale is done, some options are no longer available.

chapters.title: Deciding among several heirs
chapters.html:
Managing collective decisions without conflict.

When several heirs are involved, the decisions (to sell or not, at what price, which offers to accept) must be made together. Disagreements are frequent and emotionally charged.

  • Clarify early who decides what (often the liquidator, in consultation).
  • Rely on facts (CMA, the notary's opinion) to depersonalize the decisions.
  • Communicate regularly to avoid misunderstandings.

When several heirs are involved, the decisions (to sell or not, price, timeline) must be made together. Clarify the decision-making method and the split early; a neutral intermediary (notary, broker) helps keep things on track without emotion blocking the sale.

Emilie's tip

Base decisions on neutral facts (price analysis, the notary's opinion) rather than emotions. A professional third party often helps heirs reach an agreement calmly.

chapters.title: Emptying the house: practical and emotional aspects
chapters.objective: Handling the contents before the sale.
chapters.html:
Handling the contents before the sale.

Before selling an inherited property, you often have to empty it — a step as charged with emotion as with logistics.

  • Sort: keep, give away, sell, throw out.
  • Allow time and, if possible, split the task among heirs.
  • Document items of value (estate).
  • Consider an estate sale or specialized services.

A decluttered, clean house shows better and sells more easily.

Emptying the house is a step as charged with emotion as with logistics: sort (keep, give away, sell, throw out), document valuable items and, if needed, get help. Don't rush the sorting, but don't let the sale drag on for months either.

Emilie's tip

Don't rush the sorting in the heat of emotion, but don't let it delay the sale for months either. Set yourself a realistic schedule and, if needed, get help.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Confirm the liquidator and the powers of sale with the notary.
  2. Have the market value assessed (CMA).

Within 30 days

  1. Consult an accountant on the tax impacts.
  2. Prepare the property and frame the decisions among heirs.

Next

  1. Go to market with support suited to an estate.

First steps

  1. Confirm who the liquidator is and what prerequisites are required.
  2. Consult a notary/accountant on the taxation before selling.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Liquidator: the person who administers the estate and carries out the sale.
  • Land Register: the public register of real estate rights.
  • CMA: comparative market analysis to set the current value.
  • Capital gain: possible tax based on the value at death and the use of the property.
  • Principal residence exemption: possible tax relief depending on the situation.
  • Liquidator: the person authorized to administer and sell the estate's assets.
  • Capital gain: taxable profit realized on the sale, based on the value at death.
  • Estate co-ownership: property held jointly by the heirs.
  • Comparative analysis: an objective basis for setting the price.
  • Estate sale: liquidating the contents before going to market.

qcm.q: In an estate, the sale is generally conducted by:

options: B) Confirm the powers of sale and the legal steps
qcm.explanation: The notary confirms who can sell (ch. 1).

options: D) On the deceased's purchase price
qcm.explanation: The CMA gives the current value (ch. 2).

qcm.q: For taxation, you should consult an accountant:
options: D) Only in case of a dispute
qcm.explanation: Tax decisions have to be planned (ch. 3).

qcm.q: A principal residence can sometimes benefit from:
options: B) An exemption on the capital gain
B) Be made together, on facts

qcm.q: To depersonalize decisions, you rely on:
options: B) The CMA and the notary's opinion
B) Often pointless; light preparation + a fair price
qcm.explanation: You aim for the best net result (ch. 2).
